engines.body: Linking punches with rhythm, weight transfer between punches, maintaining stance through sequences
engines.mind: Thinking in sequences — punch A creates the opening for punch B
engines.emotion: Flow state — the first taste of boxing as a conversation, not a checklist

audience.hook: A jab is a word. A combination is a sentence. Boxing is learning to speak.
audience.question: How do single punches become boxing?

core.thesis: Combinations are boxing's grammar — individual punches become meaningful when they connect in sequence. Each punch sets up the next, and the combination as a whole asks a question the opponent has to answer.
keyPoints: A combination is not 'throw several punches fast' — it's a sequence where each punch creates the opening for the next
The jab-cross (1-2): the fundamental combination. Range-finding into power. Learned in lessons 5 and 7.
The 1-2-3 (jab-cross-hook): straight-straight-curve. Changes the angle. Forces the opponent to deal with two planes.
Weight transfer between punches: the cross loads the lead side for the hook. The hook loads the rear side for the cross. Natural rhythm.
Rhythm and timing: combinations have a beat. Fast-slow-fast. Level changes. Pauses. The rhythm IS the weapon.
Return to guard between combinations — the combination ends when you return home, not when the last punch lands
Combinations test everything: stance, guard, footwork, power, timing. If any one is weak, it shows.
Keep it short: 2-3 punch combinations at first. Quality over quantity. A clean 1-2 beats a sloppy 1-2-3-4-5.
commonMisconceptions: Longer combinations are better — short, sharp, purposeful combinations are more effective
Throw all punches at the same speed — variation in timing is what makes combinations land
Combinations are rehearsed sequences — eventually they become vocabulary, not scripts
Power in every punch — the setup punches don't need power. The finishing punch does.

coachEye.observe: Watch the stance between the second and third punch — does it hold or collapse?
coachEye.compare: Student throwing singles vs the same student throwing 1-2 — does the cross improve when the jab goes first?
coachEye.predict: A student who pauses between punches is thinking. A student who flows is feeling. Flow comes with practice.
coachEye.diagnose: If the combination falls apart after 2 punches, the student is running out of balance. Go back to stance.

scenes.title: Words Into Sentences
scenes.narration: You know the jab. You know the cross. You know the hook. Those are words. Now we learn to speak.
scenes.learningObjective: Bridge from individual punches to combinations

scenes.title: The 1-2
scenes.narration: Jab-cross. The most fundamental combination in boxing. The jab finds the range. The cross uses it. One-two. Simple. And when it's clean, devastating.

scenes.title: The 1-2-3
scenes.narration: Jab-cross-hook. Straight. Straight. Curve. The hook changes the plane. Your opponent was blocking straight punches — now something comes from the side. Two dimensions. Two problems.

scenes.title: Natural Rhythm
scenes.narration: The cross shifts weight forward. That loads the lead side — perfect for the hook. The hook rotates back. That loads the rear side — perfect for the cross. The combination has a natural rhythm. You're not fighting your body — you're flowing with it.
scenes.learningObjective: Weight transfer creates natural combination rhythm

scenes.title: Timing is the Weapon
scenes.narration: Not every punch at the same speed. Fast jab. Hard cross. Quick hook. Or: fast-fast-pause-BANG. The variation is what makes combinations land. Predictable rhythm gets timed. Broken rhythm lands.
scenes.learningObjective: Rhythm variation — broken timing as a weapon

scenes.title: Come Home
scenes.narration: A combination ends when your hands return to guard. Not when the last punch lands. Throw. Return. Assess. Then go again. That's the discipline. That's the method.
scenes.learningObjective: Guard return — the combination's full stop

reel.hook: A jab is a word. A combination is a sentence. Boxing is learning to speak.

checkpoints: Does your stance hold through a 3-punch combination?
Can you vary the timing of your 1-2?
Do your hands return to guard after every combination?

teachingCues: Don't rush to 4+ punch combinations — a clean 1-2 is worth more than a sloppy 1-2-3-4
Use counts with rhythm: 'ONE-two' (fast jab, hard cross) vs 'one-TWO' (probing jab, power cross)
Pad work is where combinations come alive — the feel of landing a clean sequence teaches more than shadow boxing
regressions: If the combination falls apart, isolate: drill the 1-2 until it's automatic, THEN add the hook
If all punches are the same speed, give them a rhythm: 'da-DA-da' — they'll start varying naturally
observations: The moment a student starts throwing combinations without counting is the moment they're boxing, not drilling
